title: ISRO Chief Dismisses Privatisation Fears After Employee Backlash Over Space Reforms
excerpt: Chairman Narayanan says ISRO remains India's principal space institution after nine employee associations demanded clarity on plans to shift manufacturing to private sector.
body:
• ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan said the space agency "is not privatised" and dismissed concerns about its diminishing role, speaking at the Bengaluru Space Expo on Monday.
  • Nine ISRO employee associations wrote to Narayanan on September 4, seeking clarity on plans to transfer manufacturing and operational functions to private companies.
  • The concerns were triggered by IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Goenka's August 21 remarks that "eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles" — a statement not followed by any official policy communication.
  • ISRO currently works with 450 industries, with 80% of the budget for a PSLV or GSLV launch invested in Indian industry. India is targeting around 50 launch vehicles per year.

Chairman Narayanan Addresses Staff Concerns

ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan on Monday sought to ease growing anxiety among the agency's nearly 20,000 employees over the government's push to expand private-sector participation in India's space industry.

https://x.com/isro/status/2096614804094099486

Speaking to reporters after inaugurating the ninth edition of the Bengaluru Space Expo (BSX), Narayanan said India's space programme is about 64-65 years old, with 56 space assets currently in orbit serving the country. But the need, he stressed, is for far greater capacity.

"ISRO will continue to remain India's principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities."

— ISRO statement on X

Narayanan acknowledged the concerns raised by employees as "genuine" and assured they would be addressed, while emphasizing that ISRO's collaboration with private industry was part of space-sector reforms introduced six years ago under Prime Minister Modi's government — not a new development.

What Triggered the Uproar

The reassurance came after nine ISRO employee associations — including the ISRO Staff Association, SHAR Employees Association, and seven others — wrote a letter to the chairman on September 4, seeking official clarification on reports about transferring core manufacturing and operational functions to private entities.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ngj6GP5iRK8

The letter was prompted by remarks from Pawan Goenka, chairman of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), at a public event on August 21. Goenka reportedly said, "Eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU."

The employee associations noted that Goenka's remarks were not followed by any official communication from the Department of Space outlining approved policy, legal framework, implementation timeline, or implications for the existing workforce.

"Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned ISRO. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces ISRO to a residual R&D boutique while the realisation of the nation's launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands."

— Joint letter from nine ISRO employee associations

India's Space Privatisation Push

India opened its space sector to private companies in 2020, and industry has increasingly taken on rocket manufacturing and other activities previously dominated by ISRO. A consortium led by state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and Larsen & Toubro is already producing ISRO's Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), while technology for the Small Satellite Launch Vehicle has been transferred to HAL.

Narayanan noted that around 450 industries currently work with ISRO, and nearly 80% of the budget for a PSLV or GSLV launch is invested in Indian industry. India's requirement, he said, could be around 50 launch vehicles a year — far more than ISRO alone can produce.

On the question of attrition, Narayanan said approximately 150 employees had resigned annually over the past five to six years — a level he described as normal for an organisation of ISRO's size, which includes more than 8,000 scientists.

Political Fallout and What's Next

The controversy has also drawn political attention. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh accused the Modi government of "deliberately circumscribing" ISRO's role, saying capabilities built over decades were being transferred to private companies "whose long-term commitment is doubtful."

For the Indian diaspora — which has watched ISRO's achievements from the Mars Orbiter Mission to the Chandrayaan-3 moon landing with deep pride — the debate touches on questions of national capability and institutional identity. The outcome of this policy discussion will shape whether India's space ambitions are led by the public institution that built them or by a broader ecosystem of private players.

IN-SPACe Chairman Goenka himself moved to clarify his position, telling Reuters that "ISRO's role is by no means diminishing" and that "the reforms since 2020 are about expanding India's overall space ecosystem." ISRO's statement on X added that the agency would "neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished."
image_caption: ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan, who dismissed privatisation fears after employee associations raised concerns about proposed space sector reforms.
nri_angle: ISRO's achievements have been a source of deep pride for the diaspora; the privatisation debate raises questions about whether India's space ambitions will retain their public-institution identity.
